analysis.one_liner: Lets service members sue the government for malpractice at military hospitals.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to let troops injured by military medical malpractice sue the government died in House committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a long-standing Supreme Court rule, soldiers cannot sue the government when military doctors negligently injure or kill them. This bill would carve out an exception: service members could bring malpractice claims over care at fixed military hospitals in the U.S. and abroad, with a three-year deadline that starts when they discover the injury, and their damages could not be reduced by life insurance payouts. It would not cover care near a combat zone. The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families. Today, a soldier whose cancer is misdiagnosed at a military hospital generally has no right to sue, because of a Supreme Court rule (the Feres doctrine) that bars troops from suing the government for injuries tied to their service. The bill would let them bring malpractice claims for care at fixed military medical facilities, with a discovery-based three-year filing window so they are not time-barred before they even know they were hurt, and would bar the government from shrinking awards by the amount of any Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance benefit [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the Federal Tort Claims Act allowing damages claims against the United States for injury or death of a service member caused by negligent or wrongful medical, dental, or related health care at a covered military medical treatment facility.
The bill expressly does not apply to care at battalion aid stations or other treatment locations deployed in an area of armed conflict, so it would not expose battlefield medicine to lawsuits.

Claims get a three-year statute of limitations starting when the claimant discovered or reasonably should have discovered the injury, and a pending claim's clock would start on enactment, so soldiers whose claims were already barred could file.
A claim would not be reduced by any benefit received under Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance, and for acts outside the United States the law of the claimant's home state would apply.
The Secretary of Defense would have to report to Congress every two years on the number of claims filed, giving lawmakers a record of how often military medicine injures its patients.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately taxpayers, would pay malpractice judgments and settlements for negligent care at military hospitals, and the Defense Department's medical system would face the same courtroom accountability that private hospitals have long faced [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would expose the government to damage judgments for negligent military health care that current law shields entirely, a real cost to taxpayers, though one borne by every private hospital and by the government when it negligently injures civilians under ordinary tort law [S3].

Judgments would be paid from the Treasury rather than from the military medical system's own budget, so the facilities and doctors responsible would not directly absorb the cost, and malpractice litigation is expensive and can pressure defensive medicine, which the bill's two-year claim-count reports would not offset [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for a specific group: troops who currently have no legal remedy when government doctors injure them, while civilians treated in the same facilities by the same doctors can sue. The cost is taxpayer-funded malpractice payments and litigation, plus the risk that defensive medicine habits spread inside military medicine. The bill is carefully drawn — combat care is excluded, the clock starts at discovery, insurance payouts don't offset damages — and it mirrors rules that already govern civilian medicine, so the balance tilts clearly toward the people it protects.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred it to its Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties subcommittee in May 2019, and it never received a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 30, 2019 by Rep. Jackie Speier with a bipartisan group of eight original cosponsors and was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.

On May 20, 2019 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, and the action record shows no markup, hearing, vote, or further movement for the rest of the Congress.
The bill finished with 16 cosponsors split across both parties, 9 Republicans and 7 Democrats, but never advanced past subcommittee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal government and its military health system remain shielded from malpractice suits by the Feres doctrine, so injured service members and their families stay where they were — without a legal remedy for negligent care at military hospitals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The government keeps its malpractice shield

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 8 original cosponsors and 16 total, 9 Republicans and 7 Democrats — so the bill's death was a committee inaction, not a party-line vote; no vote was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would end the government's blanket immunity from malpractice suits at military hospitals, exposing it to judgments for negligent care. Its interest in keeping that shield runs directly against injured service members' interest in a remedy.
Tort claims attorneys could represent service members in new federal malpractice cases; their financial interest here matches troops' access to a remedy.
